title: The Silk Road Was Never One Road
text:
The phrase 'Silk Road' is a modern invention, coined by a nineteenth-century geographer, and it misleads in two ways. There was no single road, and silk was only one commodity among many. What existed instead was a shifting web of routes across Central Asia, linking China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean through oasis towns and mountain passes.

Very few merchants travelled the whole distance. Goods moved in stages, changing hands repeatedly, and each exchange added cost, which is why the traffic favoured things that were light, durable and valuable: silk, certainly, but also spices, glass, gemstones and paper. This relay structure had consequences well beyond commerce. Religions travelled with the traders, so Buddhism reached China along these routes and Islam later spread through the same towns. So did technologies, artistic motifs and diseases. The routes also depended on politics. When large empires secured the corridors and policed the caravan stops, traffic flourished; when authority fragmented, it contracted or shifted to the sea lanes. That is the pattern worth holding on to: exchange across Eurasia was continuous but deeply uneven, and its volume tracked the security of the territory it crossed rather than any steady growth in demand.
points: The name is modern, and there was no single road and no single commodity.
It was a shifting network of routes across Central Asia linking China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean.
Goods moved in relays between merchants, so costs favoured light, durable, valuable items.
Religions, technologies, artistic styles and diseases travelled along with the goods.
Traffic depended on political security, flourishing under large empires and contracting when authority broke down.
The overall pattern is continuous but uneven exchange, tracking security rather than demand.
